extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal principles governing the ownership, transfer, seizure, and licensing of U.S. letters-patent, including the rights of executors/administrators, creditors, receivers, assignments, grants, and licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executor/administrator holds patent as a federal franchise (not estate personalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The property in a patented invention in the hands of an executor or administrator is not personal property of the decedent's estate but a franchise held in a special capacity under the Patent Laws of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the executor's title rests on acts of Congress, not state probate law; the patent does not enter into dealings with the estate as such; the administrator is often called a trustee but has only an instrumentary role and is accountable in equity to beneficiaries (cases: Goodyear v. Hullihan, Northwestern Fire Extinguisher Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executor/administrator's duties and powers re: patent prosecution and issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an inventor dies before application or pending application, the executor or administrator must apply for or receive the patent; he may file a new application but third-party rights are unaffected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Rice v. Burt; Ex parte Smith; Bice v. Burt; clarifies that executor acts as if independent owner in procuring letters-patent, reissue, extension, prosecuting infringement actions, making assignments and licenses, though beneficial interest may be in heirs/devisees (§§801–802).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executor/administrator's title vis-à-vis heirs and third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The executor's title is identical with that of the decedent for Patent Office, courts, and third parties, but the beneficial interest vests in heirs or devisees who legally own the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executor manages and controls the property and is accountable in equity to those with beneficial interest; if will devises invention, executor holds patent in trust for devisees by implication of law (Stimpson v. Rogers Smith Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: State laws cannot limit federal administrative powers over patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The official character of an administrator and powers regarding patents are determined by federal law; state probate laws do not control the nature, extent, or authority over patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly stated: patent rights and administration governed by acts of Congress; local state administration not necessary to sue or enforce patent rights in U.S. courts (cases cited: Brooks v. Jenkins; Northwestern Fire Extinguisher Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents are liable for debts but incorporeal nature complicates seizure
rubrics_metrics.description: Although patents are property and liable for a patentee's debts, their incorporeal and national (non-local) character makes seizure and appropriation by ordinary common-law methods difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains inability to seize incorporeal rights directly; execution and local processes have practical limits; historical view that patents were practically exempt but modern methods make them reachable (§803; cases and commentary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patented inventions can be subjected to creditors only through valid assignment by the true owner
rubrics_metrics.description: Patented inventions are subjected to claims of creditors only by some form of assignment (voluntary or compulsory) carried out by the lawful owner in the mode required by the Patent Law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments/orders or officer acts alone do not transfer legal title absent conveyance by owner complying with Patent Act; bankruptcy, insolvency, or creditor proceedings must effectuate transfer conforming to patent statutes (§804).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts of equity can compel assignment for benefit of creditors (subject to statutory form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts of equity, acting in aid of courts of law, have authority to compel an owner to assign a patented invention to a trustee or receiver to be sold for satisfaction of judgment-debts, provided transfer is effected in conformity with Patent Law requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses Stephens v. Cady, Pacific Bank v. Robinson and subsequent cases; the decree must be effectuated by conveyance conforming to statutory requirements (written, signed, recorded where required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver/assignee limitations: assignment requires written instrument and recordation
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither an assignee in insolvency nor a receiver can pass legal title to a patent except by a written instrument signed by the owner and duly recorded as required by the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Gordon v. Anthony and other cases; state insolvency/probate instruments alone do not transfer title; equity may appoint trustee to make assignment in owner's name to effectuate decree (§805).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments under state insolvency/probate statutes do not transfer patent title absent proper conveyance
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment made by a judge of probate under a state insolvent law or similar state act does not transfer title to a patent; a proper written instrument executed by the owner and compliant with Patent Law is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ashcroft v. Walworth, explanations distinguishing state acts from federal Patent Act conveyance requirements; absent statutory U.S. authorization, state orders insufficient.  (§805 notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: License defined and distinguished from assignment/grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Any conveyance of an interest in a patented invention which cannot operate as an assignment or grant is a license; assignment/grant transfers the monopoly as well as the invention, while a license transfers only the invention (i.e., waives suit) and does not transfer the monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License characterized as the right not to be sued; whether an instrument is a license or assignment depends on whether the interest conveyed is one to which law annexes the monopoly (language of instrument controls) (§806).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether conveyance transfers the monopoly determined by instrument language and legal effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a given conveyance carries both the monopoly and the invention is usually determined by the descriptive language of the transferred interest; if the alienated interest is one to which law annexes the monopoly, the instrument is an assignment or grant; otherwise a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: instruments rarely mention 'monopoly' explicitly; courts infer from words, reservations, covenants, and the rights retained or conferred. Examples and cases cited (§806).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses are governed by state contract law but may be adjudicated in federal infringement suits
rubrics_metrics.description: A licence contract is governed and defined by state law (contract principles), but federal courts hearing infringement actions may determine whether an outstanding license exists as a defense/issue in the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: State of Missouri v. Bell Telephone Co.; Hammacher v. Wilson; licenses before patent issues are valid (Kelly v. Porter) (§806 guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anything less than the entire and unqualified monopoly or an undivided interest is a license
rubrics_metrics.description: Any assignment which does not convey the entire and unqualified monopoly within the territory specified, or an undivided interest in that monopoly, is a mere license rather than an assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanford v. Messer and related cases: transfers of limited rights (use only, sell only, territory-limited, time-limited, purpose-specific) are treated as licenses (§806).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly indivisibility principle: only entire or undivided exclusive rights transfer monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the monopoly is indivisible, only conveyance of the entire interest in the invention or an undivided part of such entire interest can transfer the monopoly; subordinate/separable rights may be alienated but do not carry monopoly unless entire/undivided interest transferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains conceptual basis: monopoly remains with the patentee until he transfers all rights for whose vindication monopoly was created; thus many transfers are licenses even if extensive in terms (§807).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfers of exclusive make/use/sell rights usually effect assignment; lesser rights are licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Conveyances of the exclusive right to make, use, and sell (or of an undivided exclusive interest) carry the monopoly and are assignments/grants; conveyances of rights limited to making, using, or selling alone (or nonexclusive rights) are typically licenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Nellis v. Pennock Mfg. Co., Tumbull v. Weir Plow Co., and others; also notes that exclusive territorial/term restraints and reservations can change characterization (§808).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservation of rights by grantor renders transfer a license
rubrics_metrics.description: Any reservation by the grantor of rights (e.g., reserved right to make or to use) in the transferred instrument indicates the monopoly was not fully aliened and renders the conveyance a license rather than an assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple examples show that covenants or reservations implying grantor retains prohibitory powers lead courts to construe the instrument as a license (Hussey v. Whitely; cases cited §808).

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants/obligations can indicate license status
rubrics_metrics.description: When covenants impose obligations that only make sense if the monopoly remains in the alienor (e.g., covenant by alienor to prosecute infringers), such covenants indicate the instrument transfers less than the entire interest and is a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: presence of protective covenants by grantor suggests grantor retains prohibition power and thus the transfer is limited to invention rights only (license).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive agency/sole-agent arrangements and nonexclusive rights are licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts appointing someone as sole agent to make/sell or to canvass, contracts giving nonexclusive rights to make/use/sell, or granting exclusive selling rights without the right to make are generally licenses, not assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kempton v. Bray, Springfield v. Drake, Ingalls v. Tice; a sole agent retaining commission is not assignment—monopoly remains with grantor (§808 and examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses may be oral or granted before patent issues in certain circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Some forms of licenses (e.g., agency to canvass, power to sell as agent) may be oral and licenses may be granted before patent issues; but assignment of legal title typically requires written instrument and statutory formalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited: Springfield v. Drake; Kelly v. Porter (licenses before issue); distinction maintained between informal licenses and assignments requiring writing/recordation (§806–808).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of exclusive rights with power to vend to others carries entire interest
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of the exclusive right to make, use, and sell, together with power to vend to others to use and sell, carries the entire patented interest and is an assignment rather than a mere license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Pickhardt v. Packard; Mitchell v. Hawley—where the assignor transfers the exclusive franchise with no reservation, the assignor ceases to be owner and becomes at most a licensee under assignee.  (§808).
